mainEntity.name: What is the structure of a Java program?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Java program follows this order: (1) Package declaration (optional), (2) Import statements (optional), (3) Class declaration (mandatory), (4) Variable declarations, (5) main() method (mandatory for standalone app), (6) Statements and logic. Every statement ends with a semicolon, code blocks are wrapped in curly braces {}, and the public class name must exactly match the .java filename.

mainEntity.name: How many primitive data types does Java have?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java has exactly 8 primitive data types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean. Their sizes are fixed regardless of the platform — for example, int is always 32 bits in Java, even on different operating systems. This is a key part of Java's Write Once Run Anywhere guarantee.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between local and instance variables in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A local variable is declared inside a method — it only exists during that method's execution and must be initialized before use (no default value). An instance variable is declared inside a class but outside any method — it exists as long as the object exists and receives a default value automatically (0 for numbers, false for boolean, null for objects).

mainEntity.name: How do you take user input in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use the Scanner class from java.util. Steps: (1) import java.util.Scanner; (2) Create: Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in); (3) Read: sc.nextInt() for integers, sc.nextDouble() for decimals, sc.nextLine() for full strings, sc.next() for single words. Always close the scanner with sc.close() when done.

mainEntity.name: What is type casting in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Type casting is converting a value from one data type to another. Widening casting (automatic) converts smaller types to larger ones without data loss (int to long to double). Narrowing casting (manual) converts larger types to smaller ones and may lose data — you must explicitly write the target type: int x = (int) 9.99; x becomes 9 because the decimal part is truncated.

articleHeader.title: Java Introduction — Program Structure & Syntax
articleHeader.subtitle: A complete beginner's guide to Java syntax, program structure, tokens, identifiers, keywords, comments, data types, and variables — with working code examples.

blocks.text: In the previous chapter, we learned what Java is, its history, features, and the JDK/JRE/JVM architecture. Now it is time to actually start writing Java code. This chapter covers the foundational concepts every Java developer must know before writing their first real program.

Before writing any Java program, you need to understand the building blocks of Java code — how a Java file is structured, what syntax rules Java follows, what tokens and identifiers are, and how Java handles different types of data. These fundamentals apply to every single Java program you will ever write.

items.text: Java program structure, syntax rules, tokens, keywords, identifiers, comments, data types, variables, and how to take user input.

blocks.text: Every Java program follows a strict structure. Unlike Python or JavaScript, Java is highly structured — and that structure is what makes Java programs reliable and maintainable. Let us look at a complete Java program and break it down piece by piece.

blocks.label: JavaIntro.java
lines: // 5. Main Method — Entry Point (mandatory for standalone app)

blocks.text: Breaking Down the Java Program Structure

items.html: 1. Package Declaration — Optional but recommended. Groups related classes together. Example: package com.company.project;. Must be the first statement in the file (before imports).

2. Import Statements — Optional. Brings in classes from other packages so you can use them without writing the full path. Example: import java.util.Scanner; lets you use Scanner directly instead of java.util.Scanner.

3. Class Declaration — Mandatory. Every Java program must have at least one class. The public class name must exactly match the filename. Example: class JavaIntro must be in a file named JavaIntro.java.
4. Instance Variables — Optional. Variables declared inside the class but outside any method. They represent the state/properties of the class.
5. main() Method — Mandatory for standalone applications. This is where JVM starts executing your program. Exact signature: public static void main(String[] args).
6. Statements & Expressions — The actual code logic — variable declarations, method calls, control flow, etc. Every statement ends with a semicolon ;.

sections.title: Java Syntax Rules — What You Must Know

blocks.text: Java has strict syntax rules. Violating any of these causes a compilation error — your program will not compile until you fix the error. Learning these rules early saves hours of debugging.

items.title: Case Sensitive
items.text: Java is strictly case-sensitive. 'String' and 'string' are different. 'System' and 'system' are different. Always match the exact case.

items.title: File Name = Class Name
items.text: The public class name must exactly match the .java filename. Class 'HelloWorld' must be in 'HelloWorld.java' — not 'helloworld.java' or 'Hello.java'.

items.title: main() is Mandatory
items.text: Every standalone Java application must have 'public static void main(String[] args)'. This is the JVM's entry point — it must be exact.

items.title: Semicolon Required
items.text: Every Java statement ends with a semicolon (;). Missing a semicolon is the most common beginner mistake and causes a compile error.

items.title: Curly Braces for Blocks
items.text: Curly braces {} define code blocks — class bodies, method bodies, if/else blocks, loops. Every opening brace { must have a matching closing brace }.

items.title: One Public Class Per File
items.text: A .java file can contain multiple classes, but only ONE class can be public. The public class must match the filename.

blocks.text: Good practice: Always use an IDE like IntelliJ IDEA or Eclipse — they highlight syntax errors in real time so you catch mistakes as you type.

sections.title: Java Tokens — The Smallest Units of Java Code

blocks.text: When the Java Compiler reads your source code, it first breaks it down into the smallest individual units called tokens. A token is the smallest meaningful element in a Java program. There are 5 types of tokens in Java:

rows: Reserved words with predefined meaning in Java. Cannot be used as identifiers.
int, class, public, static, void, if, else, for, while, return, new, true, false
Names given to variables, methods, classes, and packages by the programmer.
main, args, System, HelloWorld, myVariable, calculateTotal
Fixed values directly written in code.
Symbols that perform operations on variables and values.
Symbols used to separate code elements.

blocks.label: Tokens Example
lines: boolean passed = true;        // boolean=keyword, passed=identifier, true=literal

blocks.text: Keywords (also called reserved words) are words that have a special, predefined meaning in Java. You cannot use them as variable names, class names, or method names. Java has 67 reserved keywords as of Java 21.

rows: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean
class, interface, enum, extends, implements, new, this, super, instanceof
if, else, switch, case, default, break, continue, return
static, final, abstract, synchronized, volatile, transient, native
void, null, true, false, var (since Java 10), record (since Java 16), sealed (since Java 17)

items.html: ⚠️ Note: true, false, and null are technically literals, not keywords — but they are also reserved and cannot be used as identifiers.
⚠️ Note: goto and const are reserved in Java but currently unused. They exist to prevent programmers from using them as identifiers.

blocks.text: An identifier is a name you give to a variable, method, class, or package. Java has strict rules about what makes a valid identifier, plus widely followed naming conventions that make code readable.
✅ Rules for Valid Identifiers (Mandatory)

items.html: Must start with a letter (A–Z or a–z), an underscore (_), or a dollar sign ($). Cannot start with a digit.
After the first character, can contain letters, digits (0–9), underscores, and dollar signs.
Java identifiers are case-sensitive. age, Age, and AGE are three different identifiers.
There is no maximum length limit, but keep them meaningful and concise.

rows: Starts with a letter, contains only letters
Underscore is allowed as the first character
Dollar sign is allowed as the first character
Digits allowed after the first character
Reserved keyword — cannot be used as identifier
Spaces are not allowed in identifiers

blocks.text: 📐 Naming Conventions (Best Practices)

Comments are lines in your code that the Java compiler completely ignores. They exist purely for human readers — to explain what the code does, why a decision was made, or to temporarily disable code during debugging. Writing good comments is a professional habit.
Java supports three types of comments:
1. Single-Line Comment ( // )

blocks.label: Single-Line Comment
lines: int age = 21;  // age of the student
// The line below is temporarily disabled:

blocks.text: 2. Multi-Line Comment ( /* ... */ )

blocks.label: Multi-Line Comment
lines: * This method calculates the area of a rectangle.
* Both parameters must be positive numbers.

blocks.text: 3. Documentation Comment ( /** ... */ ) — Javadoc

blocks.label: Javadoc Comment
lines: * Calculates the sum of two integers.
* @return   the sum of a and b
public int add(int a, int b) {

rows: Short inline explanations, disabling a single line
Explaining a block of code, temporarily disabling multiple lines
Official API documentation — classes, methods, parameters

items.html: 💡 Tip: Run javadoc ClassName.java in the terminal to auto-generate HTML documentation from your Javadoc comments — the same way the official Java API docs are generated.

blocks.text: In Java, every variable has a data type that defines what kind of value it can hold and how much memory it occupies. Java is a strongly typed language — you must declare the type of every variable before using it. Java has two categories of data types:
🔢 Primitive Data Types (8 Types)

Primitive types are the most basic data types built into Java. They store simple values directly in memory. Java has exactly 8 primitive data types — and their sizes are fixed regardless of the platform (this is part of Java's portability).
🏛️ Non-Primitive Data Types (Reference Types)

Non-primitive (reference) types do not store the value directly — they store a reference (memory address) to where the data is stored in the heap. All non-primitive types are derived from the Object class.

rows: Sequence of characters. Most commonly used type.
Blueprint for creating objects with state and behavior.
Abstract type that defines a contract for classes.
Special type with a fixed set of named constants.

blocks.text: A variable is a named container in memory that stores a value. Every variable in Java has a name (identifier), a data type, and a value. You must declare a variable before using it.
Variable Declaration and Initialization

blocks.label: Variable Syntax
lines: final double PI = 3.14159;  // Constant — value cannot change

blocks.text: Types of Variables in Java

rows: Only within that method/block — destroyed after method ends
As long as the object exists — each object has its own copy
As long as the class is loaded — shared across all objects
void show(int age) — age is a parameter

blocks.text: var — Type Inference (Java 10+)
Since Java 10, you can use var for local variables — the compiler automatically infers the type from the assigned value. This makes code shorter without sacrificing type safety.

items.html: ⚠️ var only works for local variables where the type can be inferred at compile time. You cannot use var for instance variables, method parameters, or return types.

sections.title: Java Input and Output — System.out and Scanner

blocks.text: Every useful program needs to display output to the user and receive input from the user. Java provides built-in mechanisms for both.
Output — System.out

rows: Prints text and moves to a new line
Prints text WITHOUT moving to a new line

blocks.text: Input — Scanner Class
To take input from the user (keyboard), Java uses the Scanner class from the java.util package. You must import it before using it.

blocks.label: Scanner Input Demo
lines: String name = sc.nextLine();   // reads full line
sc.close();  // Step 5: Always close the scanner

blocks.text: Type casting is the process of converting a value from one data type to another. Java supports two types of casting:
1. Widening Casting (Automatic / Implicit)
Converting a smaller data type to a larger one. Java does this automatically — no data is lost. Order: byte → short → int → long → float → double

blocks.label: Widening Casting
lines: long   myLong   = myInt;     // int automatically widens to long
float  myFloat  = myLong;    // long automatically widens to float
double myDouble = myFloat;   // float automatically widens to double

blocks.text: 2. Narrowing Casting (Manual / Explicit)
Converting a larger data type to a smaller one. Must be done manually by placing the target type in parentheses. Data loss may occur — use with caution.

blocks.label: Narrowing Casting
lines: int    myInt    = (int) myDouble;  // manually cast double to int

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor
These are commonly asked Java interview questions related to the basics covered in this chapter — syntax, data types, variables, and identifiers.

items.q: Q1. What are the 8 primitive data types in Java?
items.a: The 8 primitive data types in Java are: byte (1 byte), short (2 bytes), int (4 bytes), long (8 bytes), float (4 bytes), double (8 bytes), char (2 bytes), and boolean (true/false). These are the only non-object types in Java — they store values directly in memory rather than as references.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between int and Integer in Java?
items.a: 'int' is a primitive data type — it stores the value directly and cannot be null. 'Integer' is a Wrapper Class (non-primitive) — it wraps int in an Object, can be null, and provides utility methods like Integer.parseInt(), Integer.MAX_VALUE, etc. Java auto-boxes and unboxes between int and Integer automatically in most contexts.

items.q: Q3. What is the default value of a local variable in Java?
items.a: Local variables in Java do NOT have a default value. The Java compiler forces you to initialize a local variable before using it — otherwise you get a compile error: 'variable might not have been initialized'. Instance variables and static variables DO get default values (int → 0, boolean → false, Object → null).

items.q: Q4. What is a valid identifier in Java? Give examples of invalid identifiers.
items.a: A valid Java identifier must start with a letter (A–Z/a–z), underscore (_), or dollar sign ($), and can be followed by letters, digits, underscores, or dollar signs. It cannot be a keyword or contain spaces. Invalid examples: 2marks (starts with digit), my-name (hyphen not allowed), class (reserved keyword), my name (space not allowed).

items.q: Q5. What is the difference between == and = in Java?
items.a: = is the assignment operator — it assigns a value to a variable (e.g., int x = 5). == is the equality/comparison operator — it checks if two values are equal and returns true or false (e.g., if (x == 5)). Confusing = and == is a classic beginner mistake, though Java's strict typing usually produces a compile error if you use = in a boolean context.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between float and double? Which should you prefer?
items.a: float is a 32-bit (4-byte) single-precision decimal — accurate up to ~7 decimal digits. Requires 'f' suffix: 3.14f. double is a 64-bit (8-byte) double-precision decimal — accurate up to ~15 decimal digits. In Java, decimal literals like 3.14 are double by default. Prefer double for most use cases as it offers better precision. Use float only when memory is extremely constrained.

items.q: Q7. What happens when you add an int and a String in Java?
items.a: When you add an int and a String, Java performs String concatenation — the int is automatically converted to its String representation. Example: System.out.println(10 + 20 + ' Java') outputs '30 Java' because 10+20=30 first, then 30 + ' Java' = '30 Java'. But System.out.println('Java' + 10 + 20) outputs 'Java1020' because String + int is always concatenation (left to right).

items.q: Q8. What are the three types of comments in Java?
items.a: Java supports three comment types: (1) Single-line comment using // — everything after // on the same line is ignored. (2) Multi-line comment using /* ... */ — everything between these delimiters is ignored, spanning multiple lines. (3) Documentation comment using /** ... */ — used with the javadoc tool to auto-generate HTML API documentation.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of Java Intro concepts. Answer each question yourself before revealing the answer.

items.q: 1. Which of the following are valid Java identifiers? _myVar, 3count, $price, my-value, public
items.a: _myVar ✅ (starts with underscore — valid), 3count ❌ (starts with digit — invalid), $price ✅ (starts with $ — valid), my-value ❌ (hyphen not allowed), public ❌ (reserved keyword). Valid identifiers: _myVar and $price.

items.q: 2. What is the output of: System.out.println("Java" + 1 + 2);
items.a: Output: Java12. Java evaluates left to right. "Java" + 1 = "Java1" (String concatenation). "Java1" + 2 = "Java12" (String concatenation again). Compare with: System.out.println(1 + 2 + "Java") → outputs "3Java" because 1+2=3 (int addition) first, then 3+"Java" = "3Java".

items.q: 3. What is the default value of an int instance variable and a boolean instance variable?
items.a: int instance variable defaults to 0. boolean instance variable defaults to false. Remember: this only applies to instance variables (class-level) and static variables — NOT local variables. Local variables must be explicitly initialized before use.

items.q: 4. Write the correct method signature for the Java main method and explain what each keyword means.
items.a: public static void main(String[] args). public = accessible from anywhere including JVM. static = can be called without creating an object — JVM doesn't create an instance to call main. void = returns no value. main = the method name the JVM looks for. String[] args = array of Strings to receive command-line arguments (can also be written as String... args).

items.q: 5. What is the output and why? double d = 9.99; int i = (int) d; System.out.println(i);
items.a: Output: 9. This is narrowing casting (explicit). When you cast double to int, Java simply truncates (removes) the decimal part — it does NOT round. 9.99 becomes 9, not 10. This is intentional behavior and a potential source of bugs if you expect rounding.

items.q: 6. How many classes can a single .java file contain? How many can be public?
items.a: A single .java file can contain any number of classes. However, only ONE class can be declared public. The public class's name must exactly match the filename. All other classes in the same file must be package-private (no public modifier). This rule is enforced at compile time.

items.q: 7. What is the difference between System.out.print() and System.out.println()?
items.a: System.out.print() outputs text and leaves the cursor on the SAME line — the next output continues on the same line. System.out.println() outputs text and moves the cursor to the NEXT line (appends a newline character '\n' automatically). Example: print("A"); print("B"); → AB on one line. println("A"); println("B"); → A and B on separate lines.

items.q: 8. Can you use 'var' for an instance variable in Java? Why or why not?
items.a: No. The 'var' keyword introduced in Java 10 is only allowed for local variables where the compiler can infer the type from the right-hand side at compile time. It cannot be used for instance variables, static variables, method parameters, or return types — because in those cases the type must be explicitly declared for the class contract to be clear.
